newsitem.title: CHINA: China analyst sees LME copper stocks manipulation.
newsitem.headline: China analyst sees LME copper stocks manipulation.

text.p: International financial institutions are hoarding large copper stocks to create an illusion of tight world supply and keep prices artificially high, Chinese analysts said in a recent market study.

Private Chinese think tank Shanghai Colub Consultancy Co said in an internal report that high London Metal Exchange (LME) copper prices in January and February, 1997, had been supported by low exchange stocks, which did not reflect market reality. The report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, said the copper market over the past two months was reminiscent of the Sumitomo era of high prices when the activities of the Japanese
firm's rogue trader Yasuo Hamanaka bolstered the LME contract despite supply surpluses.

"Sumitomo took away a lot of copper from LME warehouses to send a false signal that copper demand was buoyant, which caused the LME three-month copper price to soar from $2,500 a tonne to $2,700 a tonne and backwardation to reach more than $200 a tonne," it said.
"It seems that such a technique was again applied during January-February 1997," Shanghai Colub added.
Shanghai Colub says the world market ended 1996 with a surplus of 100,000 tonnes of copper, after production of 12.2 million tonnes and consumption of 12.1 million tonnes.
The report describes as bewildering the decline in LME copper stocks from 300,000 tonnes at the start of 1996 to 140,000 tonnes at the end of the year.
"It is a puzzle that copper was in such a surplus while its stocks greatly declined."
Shanghai Colub asks where the copper went and says one view "is that the Chinese took away all the surplus copper".
The report presents figures showing China's 1996 imports of refined copper at 149,700 tonnes, with exports at 39,500 tonnes, leaving a net import of 110,200 tonnes of refined copper.
Further figures show total copper imports of 714,300 tonnes, with exports at 133,700 tonnes, leaving net Chinese copper imports for 1996 of 580,600 tonnes.
"Many analysts thought China would play a more important role on the international market after the Sumitomo scandal and some even thought China might play Sumitomo's role," Shanghai Colub said.

It said the Chinese State Reserve Bureau was believed to have bought up to 300,000 tonnes of copper after world prices fell in the third quarter of 1996 on Sumitomo's revelations Hamanaka had lost $1.8 billion, later extended to $2.6 billion.
But it said this copper purchased for the government's strategic reserve had not been funneled onto the domestic market, stored in overseas warehouses, or sold on the international market.
"We think there must be more powerful financial institutions on this market," Shanghai Colub said.
The report said once Sumitomo's positions had been taken over by financial institutions, LME stocks plunged to a record low of 90,000 tonnes.
"Sumitomo created an era of high copper prices, but the sharp decline of copper prices caused by the Sumitomo scandal made people overstate the copper surplus," Shanghai Colub said.
It concluded that "cash copper is being manipulated by some financial institutions that are playing a stock game and creating (market) chaos for their own ends".
